newsitem.title: INDIA: India's first share depository set for launch.
newsitem.headline: India's first share depository set for launch.

text.p: India is set to launch its first share depository which will begin the process of paperless trade on the National Stock Exchange (NSE), depository chief C.B. Bhave told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.
Bhave, managing director of the National Securities Depository Ltd (NSDL), said the depository would be launched by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on Friday.

He said eleven banks/custodians/brokers had signed agreements to become depository participants including Stock Holding Corporation of India, IIT, IL&FS, Janata Sahakari, Global Trust Bank, Citibank, National Securities Clearing Corporation Ltd, Industrial Development Bank of India, HDFC Bank, Morgan Stanley and State Bank of India.
Bhave said around 8-10 brokers had applied for membership but declined to name the firms.

Bhave said companies which had agreed to have their shares dematerialised included Housing Development Finance Corporation (HDFC), Associated Cement Companies, Larsen & Toubro, Tata Iron and Steel Company, Reliance, Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd, CRISIL, Siemens and Hindustan Lever Ltd (HLL).

Dematerialisation is the process by which the physical certificates of an investor are taken back by the company or registrar and destroyed. An equal number of of securities are credited to the electronic holdings of the investor.
"HLL has signed the agreement but will join only after the merger procedure has been completed," Bhave said.
HLL -- the Indian unit of Unilever Plc -- said earlier this year it would merge with group company Brooke Bond Lipton India Ltd. The merger is awaiting court approval.
Of the nine companies which have agreed to participate, only Reliance and HDFC are fully connected to the depository.
The remaining companies are in the process of setting up the required infrastructure and are expected to be linked within the next 15-20 days, Bhave said.

He said the depository shares were likely to attract a premium over the physical shares as they minimised lengthy paperwork involved in share transfer procedures. The depository would also eliminate the risk of loss or theft of shares in the mail.
